excerpt: Focus on implementation changes by hiding test files from the PR diff and file tree.
cubic now reviews the new changes after a force-push when it can safely compare them with a previously reviewed version.
You can now ask your coding agent to check your cubic subscription, manage team seats and roles, and purchase more seats without leaving your MCP client.
Once installed, cubic automatically reviews new pull requests.
To review a PR that was opened _before_ you installed the app, comment: `@cubic-dev-ai review this PR`.
Reply to a review comment to ask for clarification
Click **Fix with cubic** on a review comment... cubic generates the fix and pushes it to your PR branch.
Run a review before you push to catch issues while you're working.... review your uncommitted changes: `cubic review`
Ask chat to "tour this PR" for a step-by-step review of the changes and what to check.
Select code and choose **Add to AI chat** to ask about it with the diff and codebase as context.
**Custom agents**: Enforce your team’s coding standards
cubic can approve clean pull requests automatically when your repository policy allows it. Start in shadow mode to see which PRs cubic would approve, then switch to live mode
Ultrareview runs a longer review using cubic's most capable review models, which is useful for risky migrations, security-sensitive changes, or complex refactors.
Connect your existing **ChatGPT Plus/Pro** or **Claude Code** subscription to use its models for local reviews.
Connect cubic's MCP server to your coding agent to read review findings and codebase context, request PR reviews, and triage PR or codebase scan issues.
`cubic.yaml` lives in the root of your repository and becomes the source of truth for AI review behavior, ignore patterns, PR descriptions, and custom agents.

Create a repository named `cubic-config` in your organization and add a `cubic.yaml` file to the root directory. cubic automatically applies these settings to any repository that doesn't have its own configuration.
The analytics dashboard shows how your team ships code across three lenses: AI coding usage, AI review impact, and delivery speed.
You can export team member data as CSV from both [AI coding](/analytics/ai-coding#csv-export) and [De
The Analytics API gives you PR-level data on how many issues were flagged, how many were fixed, how much AI code was authored, etc.
Codebase scans deploy thousands of AI agents to find bugs and vulnerabilities across your repository.
cubic's AI wiki automatically indexes your codebase and produces searchable wikis, complete with links to source code, architecture diagrams, and more.
cubic exports the wiki as markdown files into a directory in your repo (default `.cubic/wiki`) and keeps them current through a rolling pull request.
You set a monthly spend limit, and cubic buys extra reviewed-line capacity only when a review would otherwise be paused.
This looks like a cool solve for this problem. Some of the other tools I tried didn't seem to contextualize the app, so the comments were surface level and trite.
Happy mrge user here - congrats on the launch! It's encouraged our team to do more stacked PRs and made every review a bit nicer.
I've tried something similar in the past. The concept is cool, but so far the solutions I've seen are not so useful in terms of comments quality and ability to catch bugs.
As far as I can see, this doesn't directly integrate with github (we currently use coderabbit on github)? Is it on your timeline?
Would be great to have support for GitLab also (have a project there that I would love to try this on and I can't switch it to GitHub)
It looks like graphite.dev has pivoted into this space too, which is annoying since they still don't have gitlab support after several years, in comparison to this product's competitors.
I've been testing this for the last few months, and it is now much quieter than before, and even more useful.
Very vague post light on details, and as usual, feels more like a marketing pitch for the website.

what I saw using 5-6 tools like this: PR description is never useful, they barely summarize file changes; 90% of comments are wrong or irrelevant; 5-10% of the time it actually spots something. Not entirely sure it's worth the noise.
When I read '51% fewer false positives' followed immediately by 'Median comments per pull request cut by half' it makes me wonder how many true positives they find.
